Hmm... that's goofy. If you've set a root password, you could just try logging in as root to bypass sudo entirely, then uninstall whatever you installed. I don't have a Mint box in front of me, but I'm pretty sure it keeps the apt logs in the same place Ubuntu does: /var/log/apt/term.log; if you installed with apt-get, that should give you a good idea of where to get started with apt-get purge.

If you don't have a password on root, you'll have to start the system in single-user. Mint doesn't by default have a visible grub menu, but you can get it to pop up by banging on the arrow keys right after post. Follow the grub menu directions to edit the first (Linux, if you have more than one OS) boot entry, and add single to the end of the boot line, and boot it up. It's not a static change, so if you can't fix things from single user and have to reboot, you'll need to do this again. If there's no root password, it should drop you to a root shell without prompting you for credentials, and you can get started from there.
Hit shift at boot to get into recovery. Link on how to try dpkg.
Did you try to remove what you installed?From a CD? Did not see a CD in a long time.

I would boot into the root user with the root password you set up (if you don't remember the password, the answer to your question is going to be "Yes" since you'll play hell trying to get things working without sudo or root access).

After this, I would use:

apt-get purge sudo

to remove the sudo package and

apt-get install sudo

to get it back. This should reset all of your sudo config files and reinstall it fresh... in case the drivers messed up this particular package.

Then I'd log out of root and log back into your user account to see if you have sudo access. If you do, then congrats, you're done... if you don't, you'll have to keep going.

If you're still not working, you're going to have to log back into root and view the apt log, to see which packages you installed for your driver. This can be done by typing in less /var/log/apt/history.log as root, and you should see (at the bottom) where we removed sudo and reinstalled it. Above that (assuming you haven't installed/uninstalled other packages), you should see the packages that the CD tried to install as drivers. Now, run:

apt-get purge package1 package2 package3

replacing each package# with the name of an actual package... you can do as many packages as you want by just adding a space between them. This will uninstall everything you list, and should get you back to where you were before your little install foray.

Once you've done all of this, log out and log back in as your user account, to see if you have sudo access again. Then come back and tell us what you did and what happened.
